notes.meaning: God gave this message to Zechariah in late 520 BC, during the rule of King Darius of Persia. Zechariah came from a family of priests and began preaching just two months after the prophet Haggai. Both prophets urged the Jewish people to rebuild the Lord's temple in Jerusalem.

God reminds the people that he was deeply angry with their ancestors. Those earlier generations had rebelled, worshipped idols, and ignored God's warnings until Jerusalem was destroyed and the people were exiled. Remembering that tragic past was meant to keep the returned exiles from repeating the same mistakes.

The Lord invites his people to return to him in sincere faith and obedience, promising that he will then return to them with blessing and favor. Calling himself the Lord of Hosts reminds them of his supreme power and his vast army of angels.

differ.view: God gives everyone the ability to turn to him, and he expects each person to use that grace to make a real choice to return.
People have no power in themselves to turn to God; God must first work in the heart by his Spirit to convert a person.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The command to turn reminds people of their free will, while prayers like 'turn us to yourself' show that God's grace must always go before human effort.

notes.meaning: Zechariah warns the people not to copy the stubborn habits of their parents and grandparents. Earlier prophets like Isaiah and Jeremiah had pleaded with them to stop doing evil, but the people refused to pay attention. Family tradition is never an excuse for disobeying God.
The Lord asks what happened to those disobedient ancestors and the prophets who warned them. Both the hearers and the speakers had died and left this world. Human life is short and soon passes away.

Even though the people died, God's warnings did not die with them. The judgments God promised caught up with the ancestors just like a pursuer overtaking a runaway. In their suffering, those ancestors finally admitted that God had done exactly what he said he would do.

About three months after his first message, Zechariah received a series of night visions from God. This occurred in mid-February of 519 BC, while the work on the temple was underway. God gave these visions to encourage the community as they rebuilt.

In the dark of night, the prophet sees a man on a red horse resting in a valley among myrtle trees. Behind this leader are other horses that are red, sorrel, and white. The low valley and shady trees picture the humble, struggling condition of God's people at that time.

Zechariah asks the angel beside him to explain the meaning of the horses and riders. An interpreting angel was sent to guide the prophet through what he was seeing. When God's ways seem mysterious, he is faithful to give understanding.

The leader among the myrtle trees answers before the interpreting angel can speak. He explains that these riders are heavenly messengers sent by God to patrol the whole earth. They keep watch over world affairs on the Lord's behalf.

The scout riders report back to the angel of the Lord that all the nations are quiet and at ease. The powerful pagan empires were enjoying peace, while God's own people were still living in ruins. This troubled contrast sets up a cry for help.

The angel of the Lord prays directly to God on behalf of Jerusalem and the cities of Judah. He asks how long God will hold back his mercy, since the seventy years of judgment foretold by the prophets had now passed. God's heavenly mediator cares deeply about the suffering of his people.

The Lord answers the interpreting angel with warm, comforting words. God did not ignore the prayer for mercy, but responded with good promises for his people. The angel received these words so he could pass them along to Zechariah.

The angel tells Zechariah to shout God's message out loud so everyone can hear it. The Lord declares that he is fiercely jealous for Jerusalem and Mount Zion. This jealousy means God loves his chosen city with the deep, protective passion of a husband for his wife.

God expresses severe anger toward the foreign nations that were relaxing in comfort. While God had used those nations to discipline his people for a short time, they went much too far by being cruel and trying to destroy Judah completely. God will hold oppressors accountable for exceeding his limits.

The Lord announces that he has returned to Jerusalem with tender mercy instead of judgment. His temple will be completely rebuilt, and builders will stretch out measuring lines to plan the restored city. God's presence guarantees that his work will be finished.

Zechariah is commanded to speak another promise of hope. The towns of Judah will once again overflow with good things and wealth. The Lord will comfort his people and show everyone that Jerusalem is still his chosen city.

In a new vision, Zechariah looks up and sees four animal horns. In the ancient world, horns were a common symbol of brute strength, pride, and military power. Seeing four horns suggests powerful enemies attacking God's people from every direction.

The prophet asks the interpreting angel what the four horns mean. The angel explains that they represent the hostile kingdoms that scattered the people of Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem. The vision takes the painful history of exile seriously.

Next, the Lord shows Zechariah four skilled craftsmen or blacksmiths. These workers represent the tools and powers God uses to smash what seems unbreakable. For every enemy that threatens God's people, the Lord has a counter-force ready to act.

Zechariah asks what the craftsmen have come to do, and the angel answers that they have come to terrify and shatter the four horns. The proud nations had crushed Judah so badly that no one could hold their head up, but God's workmen will bring down their power. God's people never need to fear arrogant world powers, because God has the final say.
